entities.label: Kanva dynasty (Magadha)
entities.ethical_notes_append: [S55-enrich] The Kanva dynasty originated in a palace coup: Vasudeva Kanva, a Brahmin minister, assassinated the last Shunga emperor Devabhuti and usurped the throne (c. 73 BCE), as recorded in the Puranic dynastic lists edited by Pargiter (1913). The dynasty was itself extinguished by force around 28 BCE when the Satavahana (Andhra) king slew the final Kanva ruler Susarman, ending Magadhan imperial continuity (Thapar 2002). These are dynastic-succession killings and conquest, not smooth transfers of power, and should be stated as such.

new_sources.citation: Pargiter, F. E. (ed.). The Purāṇa Text of the Dynasties of the Kali Age, with Introduction, Translation, and Notes. Oxford: Humphrey Milford / Oxford University Press, 1913.
Thapar, Romila. The Penguin History of Early India: From the Origins to AD 1300. London: Penguin Books, 2002 (ch. 7–8 on the post-Mauryan Shunga–Kanva–Satavahana transition).
Majumdar, R. C. (ed.). The Age of Imperial Unity (The History and Culture of the Indian People, Vol. II). Bombay: Bharatiya Vidya Bhavan, 1951 (section on the Sungas and Kanvas).

entities.label: Grand Duchy of Finland
entities.ethical_notes_append: [S55-enrich] The Grand Duchy of Finland was created when Russia annexed the territory from Sweden through military conquest in the Finnish War of 1808-1809 (Treaty of Fredrikshamn, 1809); the Diet of Porvoo secured a conditional autonomy under the tsar rather than the treaty-between-equals later claimed by Finnish nationalists (Jussila, Hentilä & Nevakivi). From 1899 to 1917 the imperial government under Governor-General Bobrikov pursued a coercive Russification campaign that suspended Finnish laws and sought to erode Finnish autonomy, language, and self-government, as documented by Polvinen and by the contributors to Thaden's edited volume.

new_sources.citation: Polvinen, Tuomo. Imperial Borderland: Bobrikov and the Attempted Russification of Finland, 1898-1904. Translated by Steven Huxley. Durham, NC: Duke University Press, 1995.

entities.label: Sultanate of Tidore
entities.ethical_notes_append: [S55-enrich] Tidore was drawn into the Dutch VOC sphere from 1663 and, like Ternate, subjected to the forced clove-extirpation (extirpatie) program that deliberately destroyed spice trees to enforce the Dutch monopoly, impoverishing the sultanate and eroding its authority over its periphery, as documented by Andaya (1993) and Sutherland (2021). The anti-colonial Nuku rebellion (c.1780-1810), led by Prince (later Sultan) Nuku Muhammad Amiruddin, briefly reversed this subjugation before Dutch reconquest in 1806, and the sultan's title was ultimately abolished under colonial rule in 1905; Tidorese overlordship over Raja Ampat and western New Guinea was itself sustained through tribute and slave-raiding (hongi) expeditions against coastal Papuan communities (Widjojo 2009).

new_sources.citation: Widjojo, Muridan. The Revolt of Prince Nuku: Cross-Cultural Alliance-making in Maluku, c.1780-1810. TANAP Monographs on the History of Asian-European Interaction, vol. 12. Leiden/Boston: Brill, 2009.

entities.label: Kingdom of Lombok (Balinese Cakranegara/Mataram dynasty)
entities.ethical_notes_append: [S55-enrich] The kingdom originated in the Balinese Karangasem conquest of the Sasak polity of Selaparang and neighbouring Sasak states in the late 17th century, after which the Cakranegara (Bali-Mataram) court colonized Lombok and by 1839 subjugated the whole island; Sasak chiefs in eastern Lombok resented Balinese taxation and, after forced conscription and executions at Praya, rose in the 1891-1894 rebellion (van der Kraan, "Lombok under the Mataram Dynasty, 1839-94," 1997). The kingdom fell in the Dutch military conquest of 1894: after the Balinese ambush at the Mayura palace, Dutch artillery bombardment destroyed Cakranegara on 19 November 1894, killing roughly 2,000 Balinese, and Lombok was annexed into the Dutch East Indies (van der Kraan, "Selaparang under Balinese and Dutch rule," ANU). The Balinese domination of the Muslim Sasak majority and the subsequent Dutch colonial takeover are both stated here without euphemism.

entities.label: Kingdom of Karagwe
entities.ethical_notes_append: [S55-enrich] Karagwe expanded as a conquest state: the Hinda dynasty's territorial growth and the ruler remembered as Ntare "the Nyoro-slayer" — who drove out a Bunyoro force — established the polity through warfare, not peaceful accretion. By the 19th century Karagwe was a working conduit of the East African ivory-and-slave trade, funnelling captives and ivory between coastal Arab/Swahili merchants and the kingdoms of Buganda and Bunyoro, before German colonial subjugation extinguished its independence in the early 20th century (Katoke 1975; Iliffe 1979).

entities.label: Emirate of Harar (Harari city-state)
entities.ethical_notes_append: [S55-enrich] Harar's prosperity rested substantially on the caravan slave trade: its economy exported enslaved people alongside coffee, hides and grain via the Red Sea ports of Zeila and Berbera, a traffic documented as central to the emirate by Caulk (1977). The city-state's independence ended through conquest, first the Egyptian occupation of 1875 under Rauf Pasha, then the 1887 Shewan invasion in which Menelik II's forces crushed Emir Abdullahi at the Battle of Chelenqo and annexed the walled city by force; the ensuing subjugation and dispossession of the Harari population are analysed by Waldron (1974). These facts of enslavement and armed conquest are stated without euphemism.

entities.label: Kingdom of Jimma (Jimma Abba Jifar)
entities.ethical_notes_append: [S55-enrich] Jimma was the largest of the Oromo Gibe monarchies, built through the conquest and absorption of neighbouring states (including Enarea) and materially sustained by the Ethiopian slave trade and coffee production, with enslaved people forming a substantial part of its economy and export commerce (Guluma Gemeda 2002; Lewis 1965). Its autonomy ended not by choice but by external subjugation: after Abba Jifar II submitted as a tributary vassal to Menelik II in the early 1880s, Haile Selassie's centralizing state forcibly annexed Jimma on 12 May 1932, dissolving the monarchy and imposing direct imperial administration — a pattern of Shewan conquest, exploitation and cultural imposition across the Gibe region documented by Duressa & Gemechu (2022). Both the native Oromo name and the fact of coerced incorporation are recorded here rather than smoothed over.

new_sources.citation: Guluma Gemeda. "The Rise of Coffee and the Demise of Colonial Autonomy: The Oromo Kingdom of Jimma and Political Centralization in Ethiopia." Northeast African Studies 9, no. 3 (2002): 51-74.

entities.label: Vesālī (Waithali) — Candra kingdom of Arakan
entities.ethical_notes_append: [S55-enrich] Vesālī was an Indianized Buddhist kingdom of the Candra dynasty in Arakan (modern Rakhine, Myanmar), attested by Sanskrit inscriptions, silver bull/Srivatsa coinage, and Gupta-influenced sculpture; its rulers claimed divine descent and administered a maritime trade hub linking the Bay of Bengal to India and China. The polity itself was not a colonial imposition, but its history sits at a fault line of modern ethno-nationalist appropriation: Griffiths (2015) and Leider caution that both Rakhine Buddhist and Rohingya narratives have retroactively conscripted Vesālī's early-medieval Candra kings to legitimize claims in a present-day conflict that has produced mass violence and the forced displacement of the Rohingya. The boundary dates (370–818 CE) derive largely from later Rakhine chronicles and reconstructed king-lists rather than firm epigraphic attestation, and Hudson (2005) reports a radiocarbon date placing a Vesālī city gate as late as the 13th century, so the span should be read as approximate.

entities.label: Peureulak (Perlak) Sultanate
entities.ethical_notes_append: [S55-enrich] The polity is genuinely attested only for the late 13th century: Marco Polo (as edited by Yule & Cordier) records that "Ferlec" was so frequented by Saracen merchants that they had converted the coastal townspeople to Islam, while the interior hill peoples remained non-Muslim — a division that reflects conversion driven by maritime pepper-trade contact, not conquest. By contrast, the traditional claim of an unbroken sultanate of eighteen rulers founded in 840 CE rests almost entirely on 20th-century Indonesian nationalist historiography (notably A. Hasjmy, drawing on the contested Idharul Haqq manuscript) that mainstream scholarship such as Ricklefs does not accept; the earliest firm epigraphic horizon for Islamic rule in the region is instead the 1297 gravestone of Malik al-Saleh at neighbouring Samudra-Pasai, into which Peureulak was absorbed around 1292. No conquest, enslavement, or colonial subjugation is documented for its origins, though the inflated 840 chronology should be flagged as a modern identity-political construction rather than a euphemism-free historical record.

entities.label: Old Pahang Kingdom (Inderapura)
entities.ethical_notes_append: [S55-enrich] The old Pahang kingdom in this period was not a fully sovereign polity: by the thirteenth century it was subordinated as a naksat (tributary vassal city-state) of the Siamese kingdom of Nakhon Si Thammarat (Ligor), a relationship of external overlordship rather than voluntary alliance. Its independent existence ended by armed conquest: in 1454 Melaka's Bendahara Tun Perak led a fleet that stormed Pahang, deposed the last Maharaja Dewa Sura (who fled into the interior), and seized his daughter Putri Wanang Seri as a captive who was then married into the Melakan royal house — an act of conquest and forced dynastic absorption, not peaceful succession, documented in the Sejarah Melayu (Brown's Malay Annals) and in Linehan's A History of Pahang. Wheatley's Golden Khersonese corroborates the polity's long tributary standing within successive regional mandalas.
